subtopic: THE CONSTITUTION-PROPOSAL THAT REPRESENTATIVES OF MINORITIES ATTEND CONFERENCE
THE CONSTITUTION-PROPOSAL THAT REPRESENTATIVES OF MINORITIES ATTEND CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 9,1 asked a question of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) concerning the Constitution. Since the beginning of the constitutional debate in this House, and certainly since the historical agreement between the federal government and the nine consenting provinces was signed, the contents of the charter of rights has continued to be the focus of political debate. If I am not mistaken, Mr. Speaker, I heard this evening that the issues of equal rights for women and native rights had been settled, at least from what we heard in this House earlier.
One very important issue, however, remains to be settled, that of the francophone minority outside Quebec. During this brief debate this evening, I should like to deal with the situation where we, francophones, living in provinces with an English majority, find ourselves in this federation, which is becoming for us a real maze of interpretations. Of course, I refer to the charter of rights, a charter which should be universally applied, but which, in this case, relinquishes the universality principle to the provincial legislatures by letting them determine how it will be implemented. Because of all these optional or "nothwithstanding" clauses, especially as concerns the provisions on basic freedom, legal guarantees and equal rights, this charter is probably the only federal document which will take its meaning from provincial jurisdictions and legislation.
In other words, the federal government proposed but the provinces dispose.
This means that the Canadian who wishes to travel in his own country will have to check carefully and practically every day how the various provinces interpret the Constitution before leaving his province for another. The legal guarantees of this Canadian, if arrested, for instance, could vary when he steps across a provincial border. At the limit, in view of this potential multitude of rights which apply or do not apply, we may wonder if we are still in the same country or in a federation of many countries.
A more detailed examination of the contents of this charter reveals that the clauses concerning linguistic rights and the right to education in the language of the minority are firm and universal clauses which are not subject to the opting-out principle. This means that the members of a linguistic minority of either official language may have their children educated in their own language at the elementary and secondary levels only where numbers warrant. As concerns the principles involved, while several premiers, such as Mr. Bennett and Mr. Davis, do not agree and say that Clause 23 will not change anything, I believe that this clause still provides guarantees which seem adequate at first glance. However, as one looks a bit further, one finds that in actual practice the reality is somewhat strange. Let us take an example. A group of French-language parents residing in one of the seven provinces not subject to Section 133, which gives access to legal and legislative institutions, file an application for a French school in their community. The school authorities, the school board answer that the application is turned down because the number of children does not warrant a French school in the area. The parents will then have to find the money, energy and support to go to court and pursue their rights at their own expense. The case will be heard in the provincial Supreme Court. And there lies the irony. Since the charter of rights does not recognize in that Canadian province the access to legal and legislative institutions in the minority language, these parents will have to fight in English for the recognition of the minimum constitutional rights granted them as Frenchspeaking citizens.
So this is in the charter of rights, a serious flaw that makes it in my view both unacceptable and utterly incomplete. Minorities are granted certain rights but not the tools needed to have them enforced. Even the Ontario Premier has no hesitation in recognizing that the charter of rights gives nothing more to French speaking residents in his province, and I refer you to a report published no later than today in the Montreal Paper la Presse, where Mr. Davis is quoted as making the statement utterly shocking to us Franco-Ontarians that there was nothing new there, the charter did not change much in the Ontario situation.
November 23, 1981

When he replied to a question I directed to him in the House on November 9, the Prime Minister recognized that the linguistic rights applied only to elementary and secondary schools. He stated that he was prepared to convene a federal-provincial conference of the type I had suggested to review the whole question following patriation. This is indeed a commendable and significant response. Yet, because 1 know a number of premiers, I am very much concerned about the outcome of such a meeting, but I remain optimistic about the possibility of it being held.
According to the information I have checked today, Mr. Speaker, of the nine provincial premiers-I should perhaps exclude Mr. Hatfield who is the only one who recognized fully the linguistic rights of both anglophones and francophones- two have replied: Mr. Hatfield, of course, and Mr. Blakeney, of Saskatchewan, who said: "If the others go, I will certainly go too". Naturally, there was no reply from Bill Davis, and I must say that I am very disappointed with the Ontario Premier's refusal. In Ontario, the province with the greatest minority of francophones-some 500,000 of them-I do not understand his refusal to take part in a federal-provincial conference which could be the perfect forum to consider and discuss in depth the last problem which remains to be settled in this country, that is, the treatment of francophone minorities outside Quebec. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Peterson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
subtopic: THE CONSTITUTION-PROPOSAL THAT REPRESENTATIVES OF MINORITIES ATTEND CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all members of this House congratulate the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier for his unremitting efforts to protect the rights of francophones outside of Quebec, for his tenacity and his eagerness to standup for the rights of francophones throughout Canada.
The hon. member has suggested a federal-provincial conference to enable francophone groups outside Quebec to state their grievances. He worked hard to get the provinces to agree to that meeting but in spite of his efforts, only two are in favour of such a meeting. Such a conference could only bring results if the provinces would agree to attend. Once again our efforts should be channelled towards that end. This being said, we have to recognize at the same time that the new constitution will do much for francophones outside Quebec. First bilingualism is made official at the federal level. Second both language groups are considered equal in every area: executive, legislative and legal. Third the right of linguistic minorities to education is recognized. I know well that in spite of all that, the hon. member as well as many others would rather see the rights of francophones outside Quebec given greater recognition. It must be recognized as well, however, that we have proved that with good will and co-operation between the
Adjournment Debate
federal and provincial governments, much can be accomplished. To wit, Mr. Speaker, the historial agreement the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) announced to the House 45 minutes ago, the agreement on women's rights and aboriginal rights. We all congratulate him. We are very proud to be Canadians.

subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-APPEARANCE OF CANADIAN PIPERS AT EDINBURGH INTERNATIONAL TATTOO. (B) REQUEST THAT BROADCAST BE SHOWN IN CANADA
CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-APPEARANCE OF CANADIAN PIPERS AT EDINBURGH INTERNATIONAL TATTOO. (B) REQUEST THAT BROADCAST BE SHOWN IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 2, I asked the Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox), as minister responsible for reporting to this House for the CBC, if he would inquire why the CBC had refused to carry the TV program which had been made by the British Broadcasting Corporation of this year's Edinburgh Tattoo. The reason I asked that was that I wanted Canadians to see this year's tattoo because Canadians on that occasion were doubly honoured; first of all, by including a separate section dedicated to Canada entitled "Canadiana", a section which featured a team of about 100 Canadians drawn from across the country including pipers, drummers, Scottish and habitant dancers from all parts of Canada, and second, honoured by inviting a Canadian service officer, General Lewis, Commanding Officer Air Command, to take the salute in Edinburgh. This year's Tattoo, therefore, was a great event in Canadian terms. It was broadcast broadly in Britain and across Europe. Canada got a great boost in this particular event.
I was subsequently told by the minister that the CBC had not been offered the BBC videotape. I can now assure him, or the parliamentary secretary who will be replying, that this oversight has been remedied and a 75-minute version of the 90-minute Tattoo has been offered to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and I and many more Canadians hope the deal will be closed and Canadians will have a chance to see this outstanding event; the way Canadians did their country proud by their performances.
I am told that the CBC is looking at a five-minute version of the Tattoo, but my view is that even to put on such an abbreviated version of a more than ten-minute participation in the tattoo would be an insult to those Canadians from all parts of Canada who were seen by about 250,000 who attended the Tattoo in Edinburgh, about six million British television viewers, and 50 million to 60 million viewers in Europe and Australia.
Canada's participation this year in this international festival has been in the works for about five years. It was treated by the BBC as a feature item. The show was designed to portray Canadian unity by featuring dancers from all across this land-Scottish pipers, Scottish dancers as well as folk dancers from Quebec. It was, I am told, a moving experience. Having paid for much of the Canadian group's expenses to go to Edinburgh, I contend that Canadians should now have the opportunity to see how well this team which they sponsored performed on their behalf.

November 23, 1981
Adjournment Debate
Last week, I sent to the President of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation a petition bearing the signatures of 107 members of this House of Commons and of the other place. I am hopeful that the minister will add these and possibly his signature to a request that the Canadian viewers have an opportunity to see this outstanding version of Canadian performance overseas by Canadian artists.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Masters (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-APPEARANCE OF CANADIAN PIPERS AT EDINBURGH INTERNATIONAL TATTOO. (B) REQUEST THAT BROADCAST BE SHOWN IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 13 years ago Parliament declared in the Broadcasting Act that Canadians are, indeed, entitled to a varied and comprehensive choice of programming on the radio and television stations licensed in Canada. Because of this longstanding requirement, I welcome this opportunity to delineate the minister's position with respect to the selection of programming within the Canadian broadcasting system. This is particularly timely in view of the concern expressed in this House now and on previous occasions by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) about the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's apparent refusal to schedule a BBC program of the Edinburgh Festival.
I would first like to comment about the specific BBC program of the Edinburgh Festival in which members of the Canadian Militia played a prominent role this past summer. As the minister said in the House the other day, all Canadians are obviously impressed by and proud of the role of the militia at this international tattoo. Given the cultural heritage of many Canadians, such a program would undoubtedly be of interest to them. However, the responsibility for the choice of any specific program, including this one, rests with the individual licensees.
The minister did inquire as to whether or not the CBC had planned to schedule the program, and the corporation advised that the BBC did in fact prepare a 75-minute program, as has been pointed out, on the 1981 Edinburgh Tattoo which was telecast in Britain and Europe as part of the Eurovision agreement.
Apparently some Canadians understood that the program was carried in the United States and in Commonwealth areas. However, BBC Enterprises, the commercial arm of the BBC, did not select it for international distribution, and it was therefore not offered to the CBC or to any other television organization. Australia does have a tradition of carrying the BBC's coverage of the Tattoo at a later date, but the Australian Broadcasting Commission has not yet signed a contract with the BBC to show the 1981 Tattoo.
The CBC also advises that its programming officers are aware of the five-minute Canadian segment contained in the Tattoo and the participation of a Canadian composite pipe band in the massed bands, and they will be looking at the program with a view to determining where it could be appropriately scheduled. The minister also forwarded the hon. member's interest to Mr. Johnson, President of the CBC, for his consideration. The corporation will undoubtedly take comments such as these into consideration when planning its
future programming. However, I think it is timely to remind all hon. members that Parliament declared that government does not and should not involve itself in the selection of the programs provided by radio and television broadcasters, whether public or private.
The Broadcasting Act makes it clear that neither the CRTC nor the government are in a position to ensure that any station might schedule any particular program.
I would like to remind hon. members again that broadcasters do listen to their audience. The broadcaster has a vested interest in maintaining and building a loyal and contented audience, without which it would be impossible for him to carry on business. The minister, therefore, strongly encourages each and every Canadian to let their broadcasters know their desires and wishes in programming matters, as has already been done in this instance.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to set forth my dissatisfaction with the answer given to me by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to my question on November 19.
In my question, I exposed two budget changes which seriously injure family farm ownership and the passage of the family farm from one generation to the next.
Provisions in the budget abolish the income averaging annuity provisions and also abolish the capital gains tax reserve. The effect of this is to impose an immediate assessment with respect to capital gains on the sale of a farm.
The budget goes on to state that there are forwarding averaging provisions which are not satisfactory when the details of it are examined. It also provides that a farmer could spread the actual payment of capital gains tax over the next three years, with interest being leviable on the amounts. I simply say that that is not a satisfactory solution to the very real problem of passing farms on to the next generation.
As you may know, the farm practice is that when a farmer puts his whole life into a farm, it then becomes his pension plan. He does not make deductions, as people who are paid a salary do. When he passes that farm on, therefore, it is important to have a scheme whereby he can use the farm proceeds as a pension plan. Traditionally, that is done in two different ways. The first way is usually a sale for cash to a member of the next generation who has financed the purchase price through the Farm Credit Corporation, or the Alberta development corporation, or any number of financial institutions. The farmer, of course, immediately has all the cash. He takes that and purchases an income-averaging annuity and spreads that purchase price over ten or 15 years. A portion of the capital gains tax applies to his income in each of those years, and capital gains tax is paid. That works very well. The other mechanism used between generations is that the farm seller himself finances the deal by selling to his son or daughter by way of an agreement of sale or an outright sale with a mortgage back. In both these ways, a farmer is able to utilize
November 23, 1981

the provisions of the Income Tax Act, called the capital gains tax reserve. All that means is that if the payments are spread out over ten or 15 years, as each payment is received, the farmer declares in that year one-tenth or one-fifteenth of the capital gains tax, and it is paid to the government.
Without those provisions and under the budget the most the farmer can do is to have the entire tax assessed in the year of sale and to spread the payment out over three years, even though if he is financing the sale of the farm to a child-or a stranger for that matter-he will not be receiving those payments for ten or 15 years.
We know that the Farm Credit Corporation does not have sufficient money-nor do the provincial plans-to provide the capital necessary to transfer all of the farms in existence in this country to the next generation. There are some 330,000 farmers in this country. In the province of Ontario the average farm is less than 200 acres, which really is a small farm. Traditionally the sale proceeds from a farm have always been enough for a farmer to move into town, to purchase a small house and to have a nest egg on which to live out the rest of his years. Inflation in the cities is high. With respect to the city of Calgary or the city of Lethbridge, I know that if a farmer has a quarter section of land and sells it, he does not have sufficient money to purchase a home and to have a nest egg. Until now mortgages back or agreements of sale gave a person sufficient money to put a downpayment on a house and, as the payments came in, the farmer was able to pay the mortgage on his house plus the capital gains tax. Under the present provisions of the budget that will become impossible and, frankly, I think we will see a very real disruption which will be a disservice to the farm community.
The parliamentary secretary spends a lot of time in this House. I recall that the hon. member for Ottawa-Centre (Mr. Evans) was here at 6.15 one morning when I harangued the government. He certainly is faithful in that respect. I ask him to consider throwing away the speech which may have been prepared for him by government officials and to tell me frankly whether the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) was really aware of the effect of these budget provisions on the farm family community. I know he is briefed by all sorts of different departmental officials. Clearly the budget provisions are designed to solve problems. I think there were abuses in some cases, but I submit that in this case there were no abuses. We need a response, and we need changes. Did the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) give any advice before these changes were put into the budget? If so, what was it? Since the budget has come out, has the Minister of Agriculture made representations to the Minister of Finance on behalf of the farm community similar to the ones I am now making?

speakeroldname: Mr. John Evans (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to make some structured comments about the nature of the new provisions which are being introduced to offset the withdrawal
Adjournment Debate
of the income-averaging annuity contracts, the capital gains reserve provision and, indeed, the general-averaging provisions, but at the outset I would like to say to my friend, the hon. member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker), that subsequent to the budget, the minister has received a great many representations, including the representations the hon. member made in his question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
I was in Regina all last weekend talking to farmers at a Liberal party convention. I am sure I talked to more than 40 or 50 farmers who raised issues similar to those the hon. member has raised tonight. I was able to allay the concerns of a large number of those individuals with the explanations I was able to give with regard to the forward-averaging provision and other provisions that relate thereto. However, they were able to put in particular questions about forward-averaging provisions which I was not sure handled the problem. These have been brought back and referred directly to the minister for his consideration.
The minister, as he said in the House earlier, is willing to look into all those areas where problems are caused as a result of provisions proposed in the budget. He is prepared to be flexible with regard to matters of timing and so on.
The minister is aware of the kinds of concerns being expressed by the hon. member for Lethbridge-Foothills. I am aware of them fully and I apprised the officials of the department of them this afternoon by relating to them the concerns raised with me by the farmers I talked to in Regina. The minister will be considering these upon his return from Halifax.
As the hon. member has indicated, these provisions for averaging were originally put in place to allow precisely for an averaging of an unusual lump of income over a period of time so that an individual would pay on average the standard tax rate to which his income would normally draw. The problem that arose was that in addition to the averaging provisions, there arose a problem of tax deferral, and in some cases tax deferral for very long periods of time, that was not intended by the original provisions. The three original provisions together tended to overlap a bit and caused some additional problems.
We believe that the forward averaging provision provides in the vast majority of cases not only an adequate averaging provision for Canadians, but also a superior averaging provision to those made available through the other mechanism. This is why the new measures were introduced. We believe they can be make made workable in a vast number of cases. The minister is willing to consider those cases where the forward averaging provision may present difficulties for Canadians.
